brief.head: Alone, not lonely
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s re­search has al­ways needed peo­ple to argue with. But there is not enough self-reflection in the world, Amit Varma said, and soli­tary hob­bies make room for it. {093-C06}

brief.head: The gardener’s firm
brief.text: One view runs a firm like cook­ing, mix­ing in­gre­di­ents from the top. The other, Ajay Shah said, is gar­den­ing: cre­ate con­di­tions, and let many at­tempts bloom or fail. {093-C07}

brief.head: Prepare, don’t plan
brief.text: Planning ex­pects order; prepa­ra­tion ex­pects chaos, Sahil Bloom tweeted. Everybody has a plan until they are punched in the mouth, Ajay Shah added, quot­ing Mike Tyson. {093-J23}

brief.head: Think like a crackhead
brief.text: Crackheads never say they are too broke to smoke tonight, a tweet noted. When writ­ers ask whether they should write a book, Amit Varma says no: want it badly enough. {093-C17}

brief.head: Shrink-wrapped issues
brief.text: Find a long-debated ques­tion ob­vi­ous, Gurwinder Bhogal tweeted, and you have shrunk the issue to fit your mind. Taking the tribal line, Amit Varma said, means not car­ing about truth. {093-C11}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma opens his Good Gyan folder for Ajay Shah
lead.head: Pearls from the cesspool

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 93

body: Ajay Shah opened with a dare. Amit Varma, he said, had once claimed that Twitter is more than “the cesspool of the global mind”. “Prove it.” {093-J01}
Varma con­ceded much of the case. Social media went bad, he agreed, when retweets and likes began to am­plify trib­al­ism and the hunger for val­i­da­tion.
But a well-curated feed, he ar­gued, gives you “the priv­i­lege to lis­ten to the best minds in the world think aloud for your ben­e­fit every morn­ing”. {093-C01}

His ev­i­dence was a folder. Twitter lets users sort their book­marks, and Varma keeps one called Good Gyan for tweets that strike him as wise. He means to re­turn to them and be en­light­ened. “Guess what? I never go back,” he ad­mit­ted.

So he read a batch of them to Shah, who had not seen them be­fore and an­swered on the spot. What he had book­marked, Varma said, would re­veal as much about him as about the tweet­ers. “The reader makes the tweet as much as the writer,” Shah replied.
## Seeing and be­liev­ing
The first was Anais Nin’s line: “We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are.” Varma called it a pro­found truth, and a cau­tion against rush­ing to judg­ment. {093-C02}

Shah came at it from the other end. He wor­ries about post-truth think­ing, in which ev­ery­one has their own truth. Planck’s for­mula for black body ra­di­a­tion, he said, is “cor­rect to the last dec­i­mal”.
Give up the up­hill search for truth, he said, and you might as well be a cat.
Varma replied that he was talk­ing about per­cep­tion, not re­al­ity. “Of course I agree with you, and of course you agree with me, right?” he said.
## Envy, courage, pur­pose

Montesquieu, by way of Morgan Housel, ob­served that being happy is easy but being hap­pier than oth­ers is hard, be­cause we think oth­ers hap­pier than they are. Shah thought at once of so­cial media.
His cure is a healthy self­ish­ness: stay busy writ­ing, mak­ing and build­ing. “It’s like I am on my self­ish project of make me,” he said. “Then why am I so both­ered about you?” {093-C08}

William Faulkner’s line about the courage to lose sight of the shore drew a sail­ing story from Shah and, from Varma, a case for ig­nor­ing con­ven­tional think­ing. “So you some­times have to let go of the shore,” Varma said.
Shah of­fered his own: “A head­ful of fears has no space for dreams.”
On Nietzsche’s “why” and “how”, Shah was blunt. “Purpose is the su­per­power. Everything else is solv­able.”
But he paired it with the Bhagavad Gita: you are obliged to try, you do not con­trol the out­come, and the world owes you noth­ing.
## What to leave out

Later tweets took in doc­tors, AI and crack­heads. The last was Pico Iyer quot­ing Rousseau: real wis­dom is know­ing which things are nec­es­sary, which are less nec­es­sary and which are “com­pletely un­nec­es­sary to know”. {093-C13}
For that, Iyer added, you have to put your phone away. Varma pointed at Shah, who had spent half an hour be­fore the shoot on calls about the mar­kets and America.

Varma’s one rec­om­men­da­tion was the es­says of Paul Graham, whose tweets often land in the folder. “Just mar­vel­lous. Absolutely mar­vel­lous.” Shah, whose picks swing be­tween none and seven, promised seven next time.

second.label: Medicine and data
second.head: Grief finds a data gap
second.deck: Amit Varma’s loss in the second COVID wave led him to a systems problem

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the missing medical data

body: Amit Varma’s fa­ther died in 2021, in the sec­ond wave of COVID. {#dad} Varma got talk­ing with a friend who had just sold his com­pany, and whose fa­ther had also died.

Varma de­cided that the real prob­lem was data: no one had a patient’s full in­for­ma­tion in one place. Someone, he said, had to build a startup for it, and he has since heard of sev­eral peo­ple doing pieces of it. {093-S06}

The gain would be twofold. With con­sent, any doc­tor could see the whole pic­ture. And an AI given a population’s anonymised data could spot what no sin­gle doc­tor can, such as a dis­ease crop­ping up in Sholapur. {#sholapur}

quote.text: I just thought that the real prob­lem here is in the data col­lec­tion and hav­ing all the data.

third.head: Read, sleep, then write

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on writing a column overnight

body: Since the mid-1990s, Ajay Shah has writ­ten a fort­nightly col­umn for the *Business Standard*, due on Sunday af­ter­noon. He de­scribed how it goes when it goes well. {#column}

By Saturday evening he has the idea, often after tex­ting a few peo­ple for sug­ges­tions. Then he reads around it, push­ing data and cur­rent graphs into his head, with­out tak­ing notes or plan­ning the sto­ry­line. {093-S08}
“I sort of fill my head with the ques­tion in a non-purposive way,” he said. Then he goes to sleep, and “when I wake up, I’m just so much more clear”. Between about ten and noon on Sunday, he writes.
Amit Varma, who had weekly col­umns for 15 years, agreed: once your brain has adapted to a dead­line, “your brain will find a way”. {#fifteen}

p2.title: The good gyan
p2.deck: Amit Varma reads tweets from his bookmarks to Ajay Shah, who hears them cold and answers on the spot

quote.text: the most in­ter­est­ing puz­zle in­side our minds is learn­ing how to at­tach un­cer­tainty around each of the things that we think are true

box.title: The folder behind the episode
box.text: Twitter lets you sort book­marks into fold­ers. Amit Varma keeps one called Good Gyan, for tweets that strike him as wise. He saves them to be en­light­ened later, and never goes back. This episode fi­nally put the folder to use. {093-S01}

sections.label: Good Gyan 1
sections.head: Part of the equation
sections.caption: seeing things as we are
body: The first tweet car­ried a line from Anais Nin: “We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are.” Amit Varma called it a pro­found truth. {093-R05}

Think of Akira Kurosawa’s *Rashomon*, he said, in which one event is told from dif­fer­ent points of view and each seems cred­i­ble. The world is deeply com­pli­cated, and what we make of it de­pends on who we are.

Memory adds an­other twist. Preparing for his con­ver­sa­tion with Aanchal Malhotra, who col­lected mem­o­ries of Partition, Varma learnt that we do not pull up the same stored file each time. We re­call our last re­mem­ber­ing, then the re­mem­ber­ing of that. “And it’s Chinese whis­pers all the way down.” {093-S02}
Hence his cau­tion: take a step back, and re­mem­ber that we are part of the equa­tion. {093-C02}
## In de­fence of truth

Ajay Shah de­clared him­self a con­sci­en­tious ob­jec­tor. He wor­ries about post-truth think­ing, where ev­ery­one has their own truth and every con­spir­acy the­ory is wel­come. Some knowl­edge is cer­tain, he said; how so­cial media changed the world is fuzzy ground. {093-C03}
If you prick us, he asked, do we not bleed? That holds for all seven bil­lion peo­ple, and is no mat­ter of opin­ion. {093-J18}
~ Varma’s reply was that they agreed, and were sim­ply talk­ing about dif­fer­ent things: he about per­cep­tion and human frailty, Shah about the na­ture of the world.

quote.text: the most in­ter­est­ing puz­zle in­side our minds is learn­ing how to at­tach un­cer­tainty around each of the things that we think are true

art.caption: Amit Varma on seeing things as we are

sections.label: Good Gyan 2 and 3
sections.head: Five years, five metres
sections.caption: reading old work, and reading wide
body: Peyman Milanfar tweeted that a tech re­searcher read­ing noth­ing more than five years old can be sure their work will be for­got­ten in five years. Ajay Shah agreed: in com­puter sci­ence, “we rein­vent the same thing again and again and we do it badly”.
He likes Emacs be­cause, at fifty years old, it has clar­ity of de­sign and bul­let­proof code; much mod­ern code is dis­pos­able.
Amit Varma added that old work mat­ters even when ob­so­lete: there has been lit­tle progress in phi­los­o­phy since Plato, and a physi­cist should still go back to Newton. {#plato}
Constraints taught lessons too. The peo­ple who put an Apollo lunar lan­der on the moon had 64 kilo­bytes of RAM, Shah said. {#apollo}
## Beyond the silo

Shahab Bakhtiari ex­tended the rule from time to space: read noth­ing five me­tres away from you, metaphor­i­cally, and your work will be for­got­ten five me­tres away. Breadth, Shah said, makes you deeper. {093-C05}

He had re­cently read a paper on in­dus­trial pol­icy for de­vel­op­ing coun­tries by a nar­row econ­o­mist ig­no­rant of state ca­pa­bil­ity and pub­lic choice the­ory, when the essence of de­vel­op­ment is that the state is bro­ken. {093-S09}
~ Max Weber, in an­other tweet from Milanfar, was once asked his field. “I am not a don­key, I don’t have a field.” {#weber}

quote.text: If you nar­rowly write pa­pers on su­per­con­duc­tiv­ity, they’ll only be read by the su­per­con­duc­tiv­ity gang.

art.caption: Amit Varma on reading old work, and reading wide

sections.label: Good Gyan 6
sections.head: Happier than thou
sections.caption: envy and the project of me
body: Morgan Housel tweeted a line from Montesquieu: wish­ing to be happy is eas­ily ac­com­plished, but wish­ing to be hap­pier than other peo­ple is al­ways dif­fi­cult, “for we be­lieve oth­ers to be hap­pier than they are”. {093-R15}
Ajay Shah thought at once of so­cial media and its cu­rated Eiffel Tower pic­tures. Our real selves, Amit Varma said, now com­pete with the pro­jected selves of oth­ers.
Shah’s cure is self­ish­ness of a healthy kind. He has things to write, make and build, so why worry about any­one else’s suc­cess? Envy, he said, is mostly a waste of time. {093-C08}
## The whole pack­age
Varma re­called Naval Ravikant’s test: be­fore en­vy­ing some­one, imag­ine ac­cept­ing the whole pack­age of them. Applying it, Varma said, he could find no one he would trade places with.

Downtime mat­ters for learn­ing too. Working mem­ory holds only about four chunks, Varma said, so forc­ing it brings frus­tra­tion. “The learn­ing hap­pens where you’re chill­ing, you’re not even think­ing about it con­sciously. Maybe you’re sleep­ing.” {093-C09}
~ His tip, learnt from peo­ple who use the cal­en­dar well, Shah among them: sched­ule free time as well as the busy bits.

quote.text: Resentment is like tak­ing poi­son and hop­ing the other per­son dies.

art.caption: Amit Varma on envy and the project of me

sections.label: Good Gyan 9
sections.head: Complain less, cheer early
sections.caption: whiners and new ideas
body: Gurwinder Bhogal, a thinker Amit Varma first no­ticed for his Twitter megath­reads, tweeted that an easy way to be­come less un­lik­able is to stop com­plain­ing. Fix the prob­lem, ask for help, or ac­cept that com­plain­ing only pol­lutes the at­mos­phere with bit­ter­ness. {093-R21}
Varma has made cut­ting out neg­a­tiv­ity al­most a mis­sion of his life. Get such peo­ple out of your life, he said, “as bru­tally as you can”.
Ajay Shah added the pos­i­tive half. When peo­ple around him come up with an idea, he goes out of his way to sup­port it; his fif­teen crit­i­cisms can come later. {093-C10}
“We are made out of the re­sponses that other peo­ple give our ideas,” he said.
## Serenity and feed­back
He of­fered a prayer he traced to “maybe some Christian sources”: strength to change what he can, seren­ity to ac­cept what he can’t, and the wis­dom to know the dif­fer­ence. {093-J22}
Varma’s rider was about de­liv­ery. As a gen­er­al­i­sa­tion, he said, men often take harsh crit­i­cism as a per­sonal af­front, while women turn it on them­selves, so rife is im­pos­tor syn­drome.
~ Whenever he gives feed­back, he said, he tries to keep that in mind.

quote.text: emo­tional en­cour­age­ment is just so dis­pro­por­tion­ately im­por­tant at the point of in­cep­tion.

art.caption: Amit Varma on whiners and new ideas

sections.label: Good Gyan 11
sections.head: Fire first, fruit later
sections.caption: purpose and the Gita
body: Visakan Veerasamy, whom Amit Varma has often been urged to in­vite onto his pod­cast, tweeted Nietzsche: “he who has a why to live for can bear with al­most any how”. {#nietzsche}
Ajay Shah did not hes­i­tate. “Purpose is the su­per­power. Everything else is solv­able.” People fix­ate on projects and re­sources, he said, but the fire is the key. {093-C12}

Varma pushed back. Purpose can be a bur­den. A long game, which both of them are play­ing, may bring no grat­i­fi­ca­tion at all, while some­one with no higher pur­pose, ris­ing to vice pres­i­dent of a bank and tak­ing fancy va­ca­tions, can be happy.
## Try, then let go
Shah’s an­swer was to marry pur­pose to the Bhagavad Gita: you are obliged to try, but you can­not con­trol what is ex­ter­nal. {#gita}

Varma pressed: does it bring hap­pi­ness? Only if you stop ask­ing for the fruit of the labour, Shah said. Measure a pur­pose by its out­come and you in­vite pain, “be­cause the world owes you noth­ing”. The big­ger the pur­pose, the higher the chance it will crash and burn.
~ Varma had put the al­ter­na­tive bluntly: no pur­pose at all, and “you just go with the groove”.

quote.text: if you de­fine it in a goal ori­en­ta­tion, then you’re set­ting your­self up for po­ten­tially a lot of pain

art.caption: Amit Varma on purpose and the Gita

sections.label: Good Gyan 14 and 15
sections.head: Second opinion: the AI
sections.caption: doctors, patients and machines
body: A doctor’s sign told pa­tients not to con­fuse their Google search with a med­i­cal de­gree. Tiffany Ryder, in a tweet Amit Varma agreed with, said any doc­tor threat­ened by pa­tients using WebMD should have stud­ied harder. {#webmd}

Lancelot Pinto, the pul­mo­nolo­gist, went fur­ther: no one un­der­stands what pa­tients are going through bet­ter than they do, so doc­tors should en­cour­age them to read up rather than gaslight them. {093-R29}
Ajay Shah added an Indian prob­lem: most doc­tors do not read the lit­er­a­ture. Patients read Google or Google Scholar; the doc­tors al­most never read Google Scholar.
## The docket and the ma­chine
His hope is AI. Research, he said, finds that an AI fed a com­plete pa­tient his­tory in a for­mal way beats al­most all the doc­tors of the world. {093-C15}

So nurses and doc­tors could spend hours com­pil­ing each patient’s full his­tory into a docket for the AI. It may be the only way, Shah said, to solve both the quan­tity and the qual­ity of India’s doc­tors.
Varma, a super-optimist about AI, gave his usual caveat. “Don’t let it be­come a crutch. Let it be a tool.” {093-C14}
~ Shah, for his part, is not wor­ried that AI will sup­press the imag­i­na­tion: cre­ative sparks, he be­lieves, lie deep in­side the human mind.

quote.text: when the com­plete pa­tient his­tory is given to the AI in a for­mal way, it beats al­most all the doc­tors of the world.

art.caption: Amit Varma on doctors, patients and machines

quote.text: Real wis­dom is not the knowl­edge of ev­ery­thing, but the knowl­edge of which things in life are nec­es­sary, which are less nec­es­sary, and which are com­pletely un­nec­es­sary to know.

p3.title: Told between tweets
p3.deck: A maestro, a sailboat, a group chat and a ten-hour podcast

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a maestro, a Raja and a vegetarian weekend
stories.head: Three days of cabbage, one concert
body: A Raja once in­vited Bade Ghulam Ali Khan to per­form at his venue. The con­cert was on a Sunday, but the singer ar­rived on Friday and was given the best hos­pi­tal­ity.
Except that the food was veg­e­tar­ian. Perhaps, the mae­stro thought, it was some Friday thing, and he ate what came: cab­bage, aloo gobi and the like.
On Saturday, the same. On Sunday, the same. Amit Varma, telling the story, noted for the record that he and Ajay Shah are both ar­dent car­ni­vores.

Khan gave his per­for­mance. Afterwards the Raja came to him. He had heard the mae­stro sing here, and there, and there again, he said, and those per­for­mances were mys­ti­cal, mag­i­cal: he had felt the oceans would part if Khan sang be­fore them.
Then came the ver­dict. “Today it was good, but it didn’t quite have that flavour.” {093-S04}
Khan an­swered with a rhyming one-liner that tied his singing to the food he had been given: *Jaisa khana, waisa gaana*. As the food, so the song.

Varma told it straight after Shah had re­called the film *Ninotchka*, in which a hu­mour­less Russian com­mu­nist in a Paris restau­rant or­ders boiled cab­bage and beet, and the waiter replies: “Ma’am, this is a restau­rant, not a meadow.” {093-J06}

~ The anec­dote landed be­tween two tweets: Max Weber’s re­fusal to be a don­key with a field, and Gurwinder Bhogal’s ad­vice to stop com­plain­ing. The mae­stro had saved his com­plaint for the punch­line.
stories.why: What goes in shapes what comes out. A host may lav­ish ev­ery­thing on a guest, but starve an artist of what feeds him and he can­not be ex­pected to make magic. This time, the oceans stayed where they were.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Bade Ghulam Ali Khan’s vegetarian weekend

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah answers Faulkner from a sailboat
stories.head: Gone with the wind
body: William Faulkner, quoted in a tweet, said you can­not swim for new hori­zons un­less you have the courage to lose sight of the shore. {#faulkner} Asked what he made of it, Ajay Shah told a story.
A friend who teaches at UC Santa Cruz once took Shah and Ila out on a sail­boat. The wind began push­ing them away from Santa Cruz, and after a while the enor­mity of it hit him.
“You mean if we do ab­so­lutely noth­ing, the wind will just take this boat all the way out to Hawaii?” he asked. “Yeah, pretty much,” said his friend. {093-S03}
~ It was an eerie feel­ing, Shah said: the boat could just keep going for­ever. Amit Varma teased him for tak­ing a metaphor lit­er­ally, hav­ing read an ear­lier, lit­eral tweet as a metaphor.
stories.why: Open water has no nat­u­ral stop­ping point. That is what makes leav­ing the shore un­set­tling, and why, in Faulkner’s line, it takes courage. Shah, for his part, says he never stayed stuck in one field.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the wind off Santa Cruz

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the group chat he walked out of
stories.head: Leave, and you’re the topic
body: Amit Varma was once part of a WhatsApp group of peo­ple both he and Ajay Shah know. All they did all day, he said, was bitch about other peo­ple.
By his count, ninety per cent of their talk was bitch­ing about oth­ers, mu­tual friends in­cluded. So Varma left the group. {093-S05}
He later came to know that, once he was gone, they bitched about him. He was not sur­prised.
It is the same habit, he said, as Twitter’s screen­shot-and-dunk, and it is deeply toxic. When com­plain­ers come to­gether, they whine all the time, and it be­comes a race to the bot­tom. {#bottom}
~ Time is lim­ited, Varma said. “Do some­thing use­ful with that time.”
stories.why: Groups of com­plain­ers sink to­gether, and who­ever leaves be­comes the next tar­get. Varma’s an­swer is to keep com­pany with peo­ple who, when you share a new idea, help you think it through in­stead of reach­ing for a “but”.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the WhatsApp group of whiners

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the podcast rule he chose to ignore
stories.head: Twenty minutes became ten hours
body: When Amit Varma began his pod­cast *The Seen and the Unseen*, its episodes ran twenty min­utes. That was the con­ven­tional think­ing: at­ten­tion spans are short. {093-S07}
He has since recorded long oral-history episodes of eight, nine and even ten hours, which he would never have done had he let con­ven­tion hold him down.

He told this after a tweet by the poet Maya C Popa quot­ing William Faulkner on the courage to lose sight of the shore. To do any­thing good, Varma said, you must get con­ven­tional think­ing out of the way.
“Too often we are re­strained by the way that some­thing is done,” he said. Sometimes you have to let go of the shore, and have faith in your­self. {093-C18}
~ Varma calls Popa a fine po­etry ed­i­tor whose Twitter feed is “awe­some”.
stories.why: Many of the rules we fol­low are in­her­ited rather than tested. Good work often needs you to set them aside and trust your­self, which is what los­ing sight of the shore meant for Varma.
stories.postscript: Varma then asked Ajay Shah which oceans he had fallen in love with. “Metaphorical ques­tion,” he warned, “so don’t tell me Pacific.”

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the ten-hour episode

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 93. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Max Weber (Ernst Gottmann, public domain); Anaïs Nin (Elsa Dorfman, CC BY 2.5); Friedrich Nietzsche (Friedrich Hermann Hartmann, public domain); Akira Kurosawa (映画の友 (Eiga no tomo), public domain); Paul Graham (Sarah Harlin, public domain).

shelf.title: Rashomon
shelf.creator: Akira Kurosawa
shelf.why: The same event is told from sev­eral points of view, each cred­i­ble.

shelf.title: Remnants of a Separation
shelf.creator: Aanchal Malhotra
shelf.why: Aanchal Malhotra’s book on Partition, built from the mem­o­ries of fam­i­lies who lived through it; pre­par­ing to in­ter­view her taught Amit how mem­ory re­shapes it­self every time it is re­called.

shelf.title: Memories and Things (Episode 195 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Aanchal Malhotra
shelf.why: Aanchal Malhotra on mem­o­ries and the things that carry them: the con­ver­sa­tion where Amit began think­ing se­ri­ously about ab­stract cat­e­gories ver­sus con­crete human con­nec­tion, and that gave him his ‘Chinese whis­pers all the way down’ view of mem­ory.

shelf.title: Underrated, Overrated, Complicated (Episode 85)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ un­der­rated-overrated-complicated episode, in­clud­ing round one of their de­bate on Twitter (Ajay: a cesspool; Amit: a gift if you cu­rate your feed) and the setup for Amit’s story of early fail­ure with Sonictown.

shelf.creator: Anais Nin (shared by @gigi_dreamer)
shelf.why: A re­minder that we are part of what­ever we per­ceive, so we should take a step back be­fore judg­ing.

shelf.title: Peyman Milanfar’s tweet on reading old work
shelf.creator: Peyman Milanfar
shelf.why: Ajay agreed at once, since com­puter sci­ence keeps rein­vent­ing the same things badly.

shelf.title: Shahab Bakhtiari’s quote tweet extending Milanfar’s rule
shelf.creator: Shahab Bakhtiari
shelf.why: An ar­gu­ment for read­ing across dis­ci­plines and places.

shelf.title: Emacs
shelf.why: Ajay’s ed­i­tor of choice: a fifty-year-old, fully pro­gram­mable tool whose age has pro­duced el­e­gant de­sign and bul­let­proof code.

shelf.title: The UNIX Episode (Episode 32)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s deep dive into the bot­tom-up story of Unix and free soft­ware, built by peo­ple work­ing for decades with no promised re­ward.

shelf.title: Constraints & Creativity (Episode 90)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Early com­put­ing was done under se­vere lim­its, such as land­ing Apollo on the moon with 64 KB of RAM.

shelf.title: Beware of Industrial Policy (Episode 89)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case against the state pick­ing win­ners: in­dus­trial pol­icy in de­vel­op­ing coun­tries has to start from state ca­pa­bil­ity and pub­lic choice the­ory.

shelf.title: Ash Joglekar’s tweet on solitary hobbies
shelf.creator: Ash Joglekar
shelf.why: Reading, long-distance run­ning and sci­ence give you a refuge from per­sonal and world tragedies.

shelf.title: Gurpriya Sidhu’s tweet: ‘Be like a coach or a comrade in your professional relationships. Be like a gardener in your personal ones.’
shelf.creator: Gurpriya Sidhu
shelf.why: Work re­la­tion­ships have a func­tion, while per­sonal ones mean ac­cept­ing peo­ple as they are.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: Morgan Housel’s tweet quoting Montesquieu on happiness
shelf.creator: Morgan Housel

shelf.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal

laughs.text: Amit ends the per­cep­tion ar­gu­ment by in­sist­ing on agree­ment: ‘Of course I agree with you, and of course you agree with me, right? Right? Right, Ajay? You agree with me, right? Don’t mess with me, just agree with me.’

Ajay: ‘But I mean nov­el­ists don’t start with a spread­sheet of all the char­ac­ters and their char­ac­ter­is­tics.’ Amit: ‘Oh my God, this is what you would do, isn’t it? Please re­main an econ­o­mist.’

Ajay’s AI sum­mary of Schopenhauer’s art of not read­ing: ‘Don’t fol­low any­body on Twitter.’ Amit, in the mid­dle of a Twitter-sourced episode: ‘All these are from Twitter. Don’t mess with me, man.’
Ajay’s one-liner cap­tur­ing the zero-sum mind­set: ‘It is not enough to win, oth­ers have to lose.’ He fol­lows it with: ‘Resentment is like tak­ing poi­son and hop­ing the other per­son dies.’

On plan­ning: Mike Tyson’s ‘Everybody has a plan until they are punched in the mouth’, plus ‘Once the shoot­ing starts, the plan is use­less, but the plan­ning is everything’ (Ajay ad­mits ‘I for­get who’ said it). Amit imag­ines Tyson’s plan for Lennox Lewis fall­ing apart after the first punch.
